Trial Oversight
The trial was led by the Australian and New
Zealand Urogenital and Prostate Cancer Trials
Group (ANZUP) and the National Health and
Medical Research Council (NHMRC) Clinical
Trials Centre, University of Sydney. Regional
sponsorship and coordination was performed by
Cancer Trials Ireland in Ireland and the United
Kingdom, the Canadian Cancer Trials Group in
Canada, and the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute
in the United States. The trial was designed by the
ANZUP investigators. Data were collected and
analyzed by the NHMRC Clinical Trials Centre.
The authors were solely responsible for the writ-
ing of the manuscript.
Astellas Pharma provided enzalutamide and
financial support for trial conduct; representa-
tives of the company reviewed drafts of the pro-
tocol and trial report but were not otherwise in-
volved in any aspects of the trial design, data
accrual, data analysis, or manuscript preparation.
Testosterone suppression, standard antiandrogen
drugs, docetaxel, and all subsequent treatments
were accessed according to local standard prac-
tice. The authors vouch for the accuracy and
completeness of the reported data and for the
fidelity of the trial to the protocol.
An independent data and safety monitoring
committee reviewed the progress and results of
the trial. The trial was conducted in accordance
with the principles of Good Clinical Practice
guidelines and the Declaration of Helsinki. The
protocol was independently reviewed and ap-
proved as required at each participating institu-
tion. All the patients provided written informed
consent.
End Points
The primary end point of overall survival was
measured as the interval from randomization to
death from any cause or to the date at which the
patient was last known to be alive. The second-
ary end point of PSA progression-free survival
was measured as the interval from randomiza-
tion to the earliest event of PSA progression ac-
cording to the criteria of the Prostate Cancer
Working Group 2 (a confirmed relative increase
in the PSA level from the nadir value by ≥25%
and by ≥2 ng per milliliter),18 clinical progres-
sion, death from any cause, or the last known
date of follow-up without PSA progression. The
secondary end point of clinical progression was
defined as the earliest sign of radiographic pro-
gression according to the criteria of the Prostate
Cancer Working Group 2 for bone lesions and
the Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tu-
mors, version 1.1,19 for soft-tissue lesions; the
development of symptoms attributable to cancer
progression; or the initiation of another antican-
cer treatment for prostate cancer. Imaging by
means of CT and bone scanning was recom-
mended to confirm clinical suspicion of pro-
gressive disease. Imaging reports (but not the
images themselves) were reviewed centrally. Ad-
verse events were graded according to the Na-
tional Cancer Institute Common Terminology
Criteria for Adverse Events, version 4.02. Ad-
verse-event data were collected during the treat-
ment period, with a final safety assessment
performed 30 to 42 days after the cessation of
the trial regimen.
Statistical Analysis
We determined that the enrollment of 1100 pa-
tients (with 470 deaths) would provide a power
of at least 80% to detect a 25% lower hazard of
death in the enzalutamide group than in the
standard-care group (hazard ratio, 0.75), with a
two-sided type I error rate of 0.05. In these cal-
culations, we assumed a 3-year survival rate of
65% in the standard-care group on the basis of
two previous studies of enzalutamide in men
with metastatic, castration-resistant prostate
cancer.15,16 Protocol versions 1 and 2 called for
an interim analysis of overall survival after the
occurrence of 67% of the prespecified 470
deaths with the use of the Lan-DeMets alpha-
spending function. Protocol version 3, which
was written after external evidence became
available for improved overall survival with early
abiraterone treatment,8,9 added interim analyses
of overall survival after the occurrence of 50%
and 80% of the prespecified 470 deaths. The
trial executive committee made these decisions
without any knowledge of outcomes in each
treatment group.

Enzalutamide with Standard Therapy in Prostate Cancer
The baseline characteristics of all the patients
are summarized in Table 1 and detailed in the
Supplementary Appendix. High-volume disease
was present in 52% of the patients in the two
groups. Early docetaxel treatment was planned
in 45% of the patients (including in 61% of those
with high-volume disease and in 27% of those
with low-volume disease) but was not adminis-
tered to 22 patients, 11 in each of the randomly
assigned treatment groups. The full planned
course of six cycles of docetaxel was given to 159
of 243 patients (65%) in the enzalutamide group
and 181 of 238 (76%) in the standard-care group.
Overall Survival
The first interim analysis of the primary end
point occurred on February 28, 2019, after the
occurrence of 235 deaths. On March 7, 2019, the
independent data and safety monitoring com-
mittee recommended that the unblinded results
be provided to the trial executive committee so
that plans for definitive analyses could be imple-
mented. The observed P value of 0.0016 met the
rejection boundary of 0.0031 for the null hypoth-
esis that was specified for this interim analysis.
The results that are reported here include 10
additional deaths (for a total of 245) after a re-
view to ascertain the survival status of all the
patients as of February 28, 2019, after a median
follow-up of 34 months.
At the time of this analysis, there were 102
deaths in the enzalutamide group and 143 deaths
in the standard-care group (hazard ratio for
death, 0.67; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.52 to
0.86; P = 0.002) (Fig. 1A). The results were unaf-
fected by adjustments for geographical region,
volume of disease, use of early docetaxel treat-
ment, bone antiresorptive therapy, and coexisting
conditions. The median survival time was not yet
estimable in either trial group. The Kaplan-Meier
estimates of overall survival at 3 years were 80%
(based on 94 events) in the enzalutamide group
and 72% (based on 130 events) in the standard-
care group.
Progression-free Survival
The effects of enzalutamide on PSA progression-
free survival and clinical progression-free survival
were larger than its effect on overall survival. For
PSA progression-free survival, there were 174
events in the enzalutamide group and 333 events
in the standard-care group (rate of event-free
survival at 3 years, 67% and 37% respectively;
hazard ratio, 0.39; 95% CI, 0.33 to 0.47; P<0.001)
(Fig. 1B). For clinical progression-free survival,
there were 167 events in the enzalutamide group
and 320 events in the standard-care group (rate
of event-free survival at 3 years, 68% and 41%,
respectively; hazard ratio, 0.40; 95% CI, 0.33 to
0.49; P<0.001) (Fig. 1C). P values for analyses of
the between-group difference in PSA progres-
sion-free survival and clinical progression-free
survival remained highly significant after adjust-
ment for multiple comparisons.
Subgroup Analyses
The effects of enzalutamide on overall survival
were smaller among the patients in the stratified
subgroups with respect to bone antiresorptive
therapy, planned early docetaxel treatment, and
high-volume disease (Fig. 2, and Table S3 in the
Supplementary Appendix). After adjustment for
multiple comparisons, P values for heterogeneity
of the treatment effect of enzalutamide were
0.14 for volume of disease, 0.14 for early docetax-
el treatment, and 0.06 for the use of bone anti-
resorptive therapy.
We anticipated that the smaller number of
deaths would limit the reliability of subgroup
analyses of overall survival. Thus, we specified
in the analysis plan that subgroup analyses of
progression-free survival would also be per-
formed to take advantage of the larger number
of events for this secondary end point. The ef-
fects of enzalutamide on clinical progression-
free survival were noted in all predefined sub-
groups, including those with early docetaxel
treatment (Fig. 3, and Fig. S2 in the Supplemen-
tary Appendix). The analyses of treatment effects
on clinical progression-free survival according to
the volume of disease and planned early docetax-
el treatment showed consistently smaller effects
of enzalutamide in patients with high-volume
disease and in those with early docetaxel treat-
ment. However, P values for heterogeneity of the
treatment effect of enzalutamide were no longer
significant after adjustment for multiple com-
parisons (Figs. S2, S3, and S4 in the Supplemen-
tary Appendix).

17|tive prostate cancer, regardless of the burden of
18|metastatic disease.9,10 A recent post hoc compari-
19|son indicated that men who were given abiraterone
20|or docetaxel early in the course of treatment had
21|similar outcomes with respect to overall survival.14
22|Enzalutamide is an orally administered, small-
23|molecule inhibitor of the androgen receptor that
24|is designed to overcome acquired resistance to
25|first-generation nonsteroidal antiandrogens, in-
26|cluding bicalutamide, nilutamide, and flutamide.
27|Previous trials have shown that enzalutamide
28|improved overall survival in castration-resistant
29|prostate cancer, regardless of whether it was used
30|before or after docetaxel chemotherapy.15,16
31|We hypothesized that adding enzalutamide to
32|first-line therapy would delay the emergence of
33|castration resistance and thereby improve overall
34|survival. In the ENZAMET (Enzalutamide in First
35|Line Androgen Deprivation Therapy for Metastatic
36|Prostate Cancer) trial, our aim was to determine
37|the effects of adding enzalutamide to first-line
38|treatment that included testosterone suppression
39|with or without early docetaxel.
40|Methods
41|Trial Design
42|The primary objective of this multinational, open-
43|label, randomized, phase 3 trial was to determine
44|the effects of early enzalutamide treatment on
45|overall survival in men with metastatic, hormone-
46|sensitive prostate cancer. Secondary objectives
47|were to determine the effects on progression-free
48|survival as determined by the prostate-specific
49|antigen (PSA) level, clinical progression-free sur-
50|vival (based on imaging, symptoms, signs, or
51|changes in therapy), and adverse events. Effects
52|on health-related quality of life, resource use, and
53|incremental cost-effectiveness will be reported
54|separately.
55|Patients and Treatment
56|Eligible patients had prostatic adenocarcinoma
57|with metastases on computed tomography (CT),
58|bone scanning with technetium-99, or both and
59|a score of 2 or less on the Eastern Cooperative
60|Oncology Group (ECOG) performance-status scale,
61|which ranges from 0 (no disability) to 5 (death).
62|Testosterone suppression was initiated up to 12
63|weeks before randomization. Previous adjuvant
64|testosterone suppression for up to 24 months was
65|allowed if the treatment had been completed at
66|least 12 months earlier. The trial protocol and
67|Supplementary Appendix are available with the
68|full text of this article at NEJM.org.
69|Eligible patients were randomly assigned in a
70|1:1 ratio to receive enzalutamide (at a dose of
71|160 mg daily) or a standard nonsteroidal antian-
72|drogen drug (bicalutamide, nilutamide, or flu-
73|tamide) (standard-care group) until the occur-
74|rence of clinical disease progression or prohibitive
75|toxic effects. In the two groups, background ther-
76|apy included continuous testosterone suppression.
77|After the enrollment of 88 patients (mainly from
78|Australia and New Zealand), the early adminis-
79|tration of docetaxel with testosterone suppression
80|was permitted in protocol version 2 (as revised on
81|November 2014) as a stratification factor before
82|randomization, according to evidence showing
83|improved survival with this approach.1 The deci-
84|sion to initiate early treatment with docetaxel was
85|left up to the individual patients and their physi-
86|cians. If docetaxel was administered, the regimen
87|consisted of 75 mg per square meter of body-
88|surface area, without prednisone or prednisolone,
89|given every 3 weeks for a maximum of six cycles.
90|Up to two cycles of docetaxel were permitted be-
91|fore randomization.
92|The central randomization system implement-
93|ed minimization with a random component. Ran-
94|domization was stratified according to the volume
95|of disease (high [defined as the presence of vis-
96|ceral metastases or at least four bone lesions with
97|at least one lesion located beyond the vertebral
98|bodies and pelvis] or low), planned use of early
99|docetaxel (yes or no), planned use of bone anti-
100|resorptive therapy (yes or no), the score on the

35|committee reviewed the progress and results of
36|the trial. The trial was conducted in accordance
37|with the principles of Good Clinical Practice
38|guidelines and the Declaration of Helsinki. The
39|protocol was independently reviewed and ap-
40|proved as required at each participating institu-
41|tion. All the patients provided written informed
42|consent.
43|End Points
44|The primary end point of overall survival was
45|measured as the interval from randomization to
46|death from any cause or to the date at which the
47|patient was last known to be alive. The second-
48|ary end point of PSA progression-free survival
49|was measured as the interval from randomiza-
50|tion to the earliest event of PSA progression ac-
51|cording to the criteria of the Prostate Cancer
52|Working Group 2 (a confirmed relative increase
53|in the PSA level from the nadir value by ≥25%
54|and by ≥2 ng per milliliter),18 clinical progres-
55|sion, death from any cause, or the last known
56|date of follow-up without PSA progression. The
57|secondary end point of clinical progression was
58|defined as the earliest sign of radiographic pro-
59|gression according to the criteria of the Prostate
60|Cancer Working Group 2 for bone lesions and
61|the Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tu-
62|mors, version 1.1,19 for soft-tissue lesions; the
63|development of symptoms attributable to cancer
64|progression; or the initiation of another antican-
65|cer treatment for prostate cancer. Imaging by
66|means of CT and bone scanning was recom-
67|mended to confirm clinical suspicion of pro-
68|gressive disease. Imaging reports (but not the
69|images themselves) were reviewed centrally. Ad-
70|verse events were graded according to the Na-
71|tional Cancer Institute Common Terminology
72|Criteria for Adverse Events, version 4.02. Ad-
73|verse-event data were collected during the treat-
74|ment period, with a final safety assessment
75|performed 30 to 42 days after the cessation of
76|the trial regimen.
77|Statistical Analysis
78|We determined that the enrollment of 1100 pa-
79|tients (with 470 deaths) would provide a power
80|of at least 80% to detect a 25% lower hazard of
81|death in the enzalutamide group than in the
82|standard-care group (hazard ratio, 0.75), with a
83|two-sided type I error rate of 0.05. In these cal-
84|culations, we assumed a 3-year survival rate of
85|65% in the standard-care group on the basis of
86|two previous studies of enzalutamide in men
87|with metastatic, castration-resistant prostate
88|cancer.15,16 Protocol versions 1 and 2 called for
89|an interim analysis of overall survival after the

4|The effect of enzalutamide on overall survival

10|earlier end point with considerably more events
11|and consequently greater statistical reliability,
12|remained substantial regardless of early docetax-
13|el treatment. This finding indicates that longer
14|follow-up is needed to determine the effects of

16|in those with early docetaxel treatment. Our cur-
17|rent data support the claim that early enzalu-
18|tamide prolongs survival within 3 years in the
19|entire trial population but provide limited sup-
20|port that it prolongs overall survival within 3 years
21|in patients who received early docetaxel treatment.
22|The main limitations of this trial are conse-
23|quences of the detection of evidence of benefit at
24|the first planned interim analysis. This early analy-
25|sis may have overestimated the eventual treatment
26|benefit.20 There was no central review of actual
27|imaging, but this factor would have no effect on
28|the rate of death, the primary end point. The me-
29|dian follow-up of 34 months is sufficient to pro-
30|vide evidence about the effects within this interval
31|but not beyond it. The sample size and number
32|of events allow for strong conclusions about the
33|effects of enzalutamide on survival in the entire
34|trial population and the effects on progression-
35|free survival in some subgroups; however, we
36|cannot determine the effects on overall survival
37|in any of the prespecified subgroups.
38|In conclusion, in men with metastatic hor-
39|mone-sensitive prostate cancer receiving testos-

41|resulted in longer overall survival, PSA progres-
42|sion-free survival, and clinical progression-free

44|nonsteroidal antiandrogen therapy. However,

48|early docetaxel treatment, the addition of enzalu-

4|The baseline characteristics of all the patients
5|are summarized in Table 1 and detailed in the
6|Supplementary Appendix. High-volume disease
7|was present in 52% of the patients in the two
8|groups. Early docetaxel treatment was planned
9|in 45% of the patients (including in 61% of those
10|with high-volume disease and in 27% of those
11|with low-volume disease) but was not adminis-
12|tered to 22 patients, 11 in each of the randomly
13|assigned treatment groups. The full planned
14|course of six cycles of docetaxel was given to 159
15|of 243 patients (65%) in the enzalutamide group
16|and 181 of 238 (76%) in the standard-care group.
17|Overall Survival
18|The first interim analysis of the primary end
19|point occurred on February 28, 2019, after the
20|occurrence of 235 deaths. On March 7, 2019, the
21|independent data and safety monitoring com-
22|mittee recommended that the unblinded results
23|be provided to the trial executive committee so
24|that plans for definitive analyses could be imple-
25|mented. The observed P value of 0.0016 met the
26|rejection boundary of 0.0031 for the null hypoth-
27|esis that was specified for this interim analysis.
28|The results that are reported here include 10
29|additional deaths (for a total of 245) after a re-
30|view to ascertain the survival status of all the
31|patients as of February 28, 2019, after a median
32|follow-up of 34 months.
33|At the time of this analysis, there were 102
34|deaths in the enzalutamide group and 143 deaths
35|in the standard-care group (hazard ratio for
36|death, 0.67; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.52 to
37|0.86; P = 0.002) (Fig. 1A). The results were unaf-
38|fected by adjustments for geographical region,
39|volume of disease, use of early docetaxel treat-
40|ment, bone antiresorptive therapy, and coexisting
41|conditions. The median survival time was not yet
42|estimable in either trial group. The Kaplan-Meier
43|estimates of overall survival at 3 years were 80%
44|(based on 94 events) in the enzalutamide group
45|and 72% (based on 130 events) in the standard-
46|care group.
47|Progression-free Survival
48|The effects of enzalutamide on PSA progression-
49|free survival and clinical progression-free survival
50|were larger than its effect on overall survival. For
51|PSA progression-free survival, there were 174
52|events in the enzalutamide group and 333 events
53|in the standard-care group (rate of event-free
54|survival at 3 years, 67% and 37% respectively;
55|hazard ratio, 0.39; 95% CI, 0.33 to 0.47; P<0.001)
56|(Fig. 1B). For clinical progression-free survival,
57|there were 167 events in the enzalutamide group
58|and 320 events in the standard-care group (rate
59|of event-free survival at 3 years, 68% and 41%,
60|respectively; hazard ratio, 0.40; 95% CI, 0.33 to
61|0.49; P<0.001) (Fig. 1C). P values for analyses of
62|the between-group difference in PSA progres-
63|sion-free survival and clinical progression-free
64|survival remained highly significant after adjust-
65|ment for multiple comparisons.

67|The effects of enzalutamide on overall survival
68|were smaller among the patients in the stratified
69|subgroups with respect to bone antiresorptive
70|therapy, planned early docetaxel treatment, and
71|high-volume disease (Fig. 2, and Table S3 in the
72|Supplementary Appendix). After adjustment for
73|multiple comparisons, P values for heterogeneity
74|of the treatment effect of enzalutamide were
75|0.14 for volume of disease, 0.14 for early docetax-
76|el treatment, and 0.06 for the use of bone anti-
77|resorptive therapy.
78|We anticipated that the smaller number of
79|deaths would limit the reliability of subgroup

Trial Oversight
The trial was led by the Australian and New
Zealand Urogenital and Prostate Cancer Trials
Group (ANZUP) and the National Health and
Medical Research Council (NHMRC) Clinical
Trials Centre, University of Sydney. Regional
sponsorship and coordination was performed by
Cancer Trials Ireland in Ireland and the United
Kingdom, the Canadian Cancer Trials Group in
Canada, and the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute
in the United States. The trial was designed by the
ANZUP investigators. Data were collected and
analyzed by the NHMRC Clinical Trials Centre.
The authors were solely responsible for the writ-
ing of the manuscript.
Astellas Pharma provided enzalutamide and
financial support for trial conduct; representa-
tives of the company reviewed drafts of the pro-
tocol and trial report but were not otherwise in-
volved in any aspects of the trial design, data
accrual, data analysis, or manuscript preparation.
Testosterone suppression, standard antiandrogen
drugs, docetaxel, and all subsequent treatments
were accessed according to local standard prac-
tice. The authors vouch for the accuracy and
completeness of the reported data and for the
fidelity of the trial to the protocol.
An independent data and safety monitoring
committee reviewed the progress and results of
the trial. The trial was conducted in accordance
with the principles of Good Clinical Practice
guidelines and the Declaration of Helsinki. The
protocol was independently reviewed and ap-
proved as required at each participating institu-
tion. All the patients provided written informed
consent.
End Points
The primary end point of overall survival was
measured as the interval from randomization to
death from any cause or to the date at which the
patient was last known to be alive. The second-
ary end point of PSA progression-free survival
was measured as the interval from randomiza-
tion to the earliest event of PSA progression ac-
cording to the criteria of the Prostate Cancer
Working Group 2 (a confirmed relative increase
in the PSA level from the nadir value by ≥25%
and by ≥2 ng per milliliter),18 clinical progres-
sion, death from any cause, or the last known
date of follow-up without PSA progression. The
secondary end point of clinical progression was
defined as the earliest sign of radiographic pro-
gression according to the criteria of the Prostate
Cancer Working Group 2 for bone lesions and
the Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tu-
mors, version 1.1,19 for soft-tissue lesions; the
development of symptoms attributable to cancer
progression; or the initiation of another antican-
cer treatment for prostate cancer. Imaging by
means of CT and bone scanning was recom-
mended to confirm clinical suspicion of pro-
gressive disease. Imaging reports (but not the
images themselves) were reviewed centrally. Ad-
verse events were graded according to the Na-
tional Cancer Institute Common Terminology
Criteria for Adverse Events, version 4.02. Ad-
verse-event data were collected during the treat-
ment period, with a final safety assessment
performed 30 to 42 days after the cessation of
the trial regimen.
Statistical Analysis
We determined that the enrollment of 1100 pa-
tients (with 470 deaths) would provide a power
of at least 80% to detect a 25% lower hazard of
death in the enzalutamide group than in the
standard-care group (hazard ratio, 0.75), with a
two-sided type I error rate of 0.05. In these cal-
culations, we assumed a 3-year survival rate of
65% in the standard-care group on the basis of
two previous studies of enzalutamide in men
with metastatic, castration-resistant prostate
cancer.15,16 Protocol versions 1 and 2 called for
an interim analysis of overall survival after the
occurrence of 67% of the prespecified 470
deaths with the use of the Lan-DeMets alpha-
spending function. Protocol version 3, which
was written after external evidence became
available for improved overall survival with early
abiraterone treatment,8,9 added interim analyses
of overall survival after the occurrence of 50%
and 80% of the prespecified 470 deaths. The
trial executive committee made these decisions
without any knowledge of outcomes in each
treatment group.

The baseline characteristics of all the patients
are summarized in Table 1 and detailed in the
Supplementary Appendix. High-volume disease
was present in 52% of the patients in the two
groups. Early docetaxel treatment was planned
in 45% of the patients (including in 61% of those
with high-volume disease and in 27% of those
with low-volume disease) but was not adminis-
tered to 22 patients, 11 in each of the randomly
assigned treatment groups. The full planned
course of six cycles of docetaxel was given to 159
of 243 patients (65%) in the enzalutamide group
and 181 of 238 (76%) in the standard-care group.
Overall Survival
The first interim analysis of the primary end
point occurred on February 28, 2019, after the
occurrence of 235 deaths. On March 7, 2019, the
independent data and safety monitoring com-
mittee recommended that the unblinded results
be provided to the trial executive committee so
that plans for definitive analyses could be imple-
mented. The observed P value of 0.0016 met the
rejection boundary of 0.0031 for the null hypoth-
esis that was specified for this interim analysis.
The results that are reported here include 10
additional deaths (for a total of 245) after a re-
view to ascertain the survival status of all the
patients as of February 28, 2019, after a median
follow-up of 34 months.
At the time of this analysis, there were 102
deaths in the enzalutamide group and 143 deaths
in the standard-care group (hazard ratio for
death, 0.67; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.52 to
0.86; P = 0.002) (Fig. 1A). The results were unaf-
fected by adjustments for geographical region,
volume of disease, use of early docetaxel treat-
ment, bone antiresorptive therapy, and coexisting
conditions. The median survival time was not yet
estimable in either trial group. The Kaplan-Meier
estimates of overall survival at 3 years were 80%
(based on 94 events) in the enzalutamide group
and 72% (based on 130 events) in the standard-
care group.
Progression-free Survival
The effects of enzalutamide on PSA progression-
free survival and clinical progression-free survival
were larger than its effect on overall survival. For
PSA progression-free survival, there were 174
events in the enzalutamide group and 333 events
in the standard-care group (rate of event-free
survival at 3 years, 67% and 37% respectively;
hazard ratio, 0.39; 95% CI, 0.33 to 0.47; P<0.001)
(Fig. 1B). For clinical progression-free survival,
there were 167 events in the enzalutamide group
and 320 events in the standard-care group (rate
of event-free survival at 3 years, 68% and 41%,
respectively; hazard ratio, 0.40; 95% CI, 0.33 to
0.49; P<0.001) (Fig. 1C). P values for analyses of
the between-group difference in PSA progres-
sion-free survival and clinical progression-free
survival remained highly significant after adjust-
ment for multiple comparisons.
Subgroup Analyses
The effects of enzalutamide on overall survival
were smaller among the patients in the stratified
subgroups with respect to bone antiresorptive
therapy, planned early docetaxel treatment, and
high-volume disease (Fig. 2, and Table S3 in the
Supplementary Appendix). After adjustment for
multiple comparisons, P values for heterogeneity
of the treatment effect of enzalutamide were
0.14 for volume of disease, 0.14 for early docetax-
el treatment, and 0.06 for the use of bone anti-
resorptive therapy.
We anticipated that the smaller number of

The primary end point of overall survival was
measured as the interval from randomization to
death from any cause or to the date at which the
patient was last known to be alive. The second-

was measured as the interval from randomiza-
tion to the earliest event of PSA progression ac-
cording to the criteria of the Prostate Cancer

in the PSA level from the nadir value by ≥25%
and by ≥2 ng per milliliter),18 clinical progres-
sion, death from any cause, or the last known
date of follow-up without PSA progression. The
secondary end point of clinical progression was
defined as the earliest sign of radiographic pro-
gression according to the criteria of the Prostate
Cancer Working Group 2 for bone lesions and
the Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tu-
mors, version 1.1,19 for soft-tissue lesions; the

means of CT and bone scanning was recom-

and 80% of the prespecified 470 deaths. The
trial executive committee made these decisions
without any knowledge of outcomes in each
treatment group.

Trial Oversight
The trial was led by the Australian and New
Zealand Urogenital and Prostate Cancer Trials
Group (ANZUP) and the National Health and
Medical Research Council (NHMRC) Clinical
Trials Centre, University of Sydney. Regional
sponsorship and coordination was performed by
Cancer Trials Ireland in Ireland and the United
Kingdom, the Canadian Cancer Trials Group in
Canada, and the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute
in the United States. The trial was designed by the
ANZUP investigators. Data were collected and
analyzed by the NHMRC Clinical Trials Centre.
The authors were solely responsible for the writ-
ing of the manuscript.
Astellas Pharma provided enzalutamide and
financial support for trial conduct; representa-
tives of the company reviewed drafts of the pro-
tocol and trial report but were not otherwise in-
volved in any aspects of the trial design, data
accrual, data analysis, or manuscript preparation.
Testosterone suppression, standard antiandrogen
drugs, docetaxel, and all subsequent treatments
were accessed according to local standard prac-
tice. The authors vouch for the accuracy and
completeness of the reported data and for the
fidelity of the trial to the protocol.
An independent data and safety monitoring
committee reviewed the progress and results of
the trial. The trial was conducted in accordance
with the principles of Good Clinical Practice
guidelines and the Declaration of Helsinki. The
protocol was independently reviewed and ap-
proved as required at each participating institu-
tion. All the patients provided written informed
consent.
End Points
The primary end point of overall survival was
measured as the interval from randomization to
death from any cause or to the date at which the
patient was last known to be alive. The second-
ary end point of PSA progression-free survival
was measured as the interval from randomiza-
tion to the earliest event of PSA progression ac-
cording to the criteria of the Prostate Cancer
Working Group 2 (a confirmed relative increase
in the PSA level from the nadir value by ≥25%
and by ≥2 ng per milliliter),18 clinical progres-
sion, death from any cause, or the last known
date of follow-up without PSA progression. The
secondary end point of clinical progression was
defined as the earliest sign of radiographic pro-
gression according to the criteria of the Prostate
Cancer Working Group 2 for bone lesions and
the Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tu-
mors, version 1.1,19 for soft-tissue lesions; the
development of symptoms attributable to cancer
progression; or the initiation of another antican-
cer treatment for prostate cancer. Imaging by
means of CT and bone scanning was recom-
mended to confirm clinical suspicion of pro-
gressive disease. Imaging reports (but not the
images themselves) were reviewed centrally. Ad-
verse events were graded according to the Na-
tional Cancer Institute Common Terminology
Criteria for Adverse Events, version 4.02. Ad-
verse-event data were collected during the treat-
ment period, with a final safety assessment
performed 30 to 42 days after the cessation of
the trial regimen.
Statistical Analysis
We determined that the enrollment of 1100 pa-
tients (with 470 deaths) would provide a power
of at least 80% to detect a 25% lower hazard of
death in the enzalutamide group than in the
standard-care group (hazard ratio, 0.75), with a
two-sided type I error rate of 0.05. In these cal-
culations, we assumed a 3-year survival rate of
65% in the standard-care group on the basis of
two previous studies of enzalutamide in men
with metastatic, castration-resistant prostate
cancer.15,16 Protocol versions 1 and 2 called for
an interim analysis of overall survival after the
occurrence of 67% of the prespecified 470
deaths with the use of the Lan-DeMets alpha-
spending function. Protocol version 3, which
was written after external evidence became
available for improved overall survival with early
abiraterone treatment,8,9 added interim analyses
of overall survival after the occurrence of 50%
and 80% of the prespecified 470 deaths. The
trial executive committee made these decisions
without any knowledge of outcomes in each
treatment group.

The baseline characteristics of all the patients
are summarized in Table 1 and detailed in the
Supplementary Appendix. High-volume disease
was present in 52% of the patients in the two
groups. Early docetaxel treatment was planned
in 45% of the patients (including in 61% of those
with high-volume disease and in 27% of those
with low-volume disease) but was not adminis-
tered to 22 patients, 11 in each of the randomly
assigned treatment groups. The full planned
course of six cycles of docetaxel was given to 159
of 243 patients (65%) in the enzalutamide group
and 181 of 238 (76%) in the standard-care group.
Overall Survival
The first interim analysis of the primary end
point occurred on February 28, 2019, after the
occurrence of 235 deaths. On March 7, 2019, the
independent data and safety monitoring com-
mittee recommended that the unblinded results
be provided to the trial executive committee so
that plans for definitive analyses could be imple-
mented. The observed P value of 0.0016 met the
rejection boundary of 0.0031 for the null hypoth-
esis that was specified for this interim analysis.
The results that are reported here include 10
additional deaths (for a total of 245) after a re-
view to ascertain the survival status of all the
patients as of February 28, 2019, after a median
follow-up of 34 months.
At the time of this analysis, there were 102
deaths in the enzalutamide group and 143 deaths
in the standard-care group (hazard ratio for
death, 0.67; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.52 to
0.86; P = 0.002) (Fig. 1A). The results were unaf-
fected by adjustments for geographical region,
volume of disease, use of early docetaxel treat-
ment, bone antiresorptive therapy, and coexisting
conditions. The median survival time was not yet
estimable in either trial group. The Kaplan-Meier
estimates of overall survival at 3 years were 80%
(based on 94 events) in the enzalutamide group
and 72% (based on 130 events) in the standard-
care group.
Progression-free Survival
The effects of enzalutamide on PSA progression-
free survival and clinical progression-free survival
were larger than its effect on overall survival. For
PSA progression-free survival, there were 174
events in the enzalutamide group and 333 events
in the standard-care group (rate of event-free
survival at 3 years, 67% and 37% respectively;
hazard ratio, 0.39; 95% CI, 0.33 to 0.47; P<0.001)
(Fig. 1B). For clinical progression-free survival,
there were 167 events in the enzalutamide group
and 320 events in the standard-care group (rate
of event-free survival at 3 years, 68% and 41%,
respectively; hazard ratio, 0.40; 95% CI, 0.33 to
0.49; P<0.001) (Fig. 1C). P values for analyses of
the between-group difference in PSA progres-
sion-free survival and clinical progression-free
survival remained highly significant after adjust-
ment for multiple comparisons.
Subgroup Analyses
The effects of enzalutamide on overall survival
were smaller among the patients in the stratified
subgroups with respect to bone antiresorptive
therapy, planned early docetaxel treatment, and
high-volume disease (Fig. 2, and Table S3 in the
Supplementary Appendix). After adjustment for
multiple comparisons, P values for heterogeneity
of the treatment effect of enzalutamide were
0.14 for volume of disease, 0.14 for early docetax-
el treatment, and 0.06 for the use of bone anti-
resorptive therapy.
We anticipated that the smaller number of
deaths would limit the reliability of subgroup
analyses of overall survival. Thus, we specified
in the analysis plan that subgroup analyses of
progression-free survival would also be per-
formed to take advantage of the larger number
of events for this secondary end point. The ef-
fects of enzalutamide on clinical progression-
free survival were noted in all predefined sub-
groups, including those with early docetaxel
treatment (Fig. 3, and Fig. S2 in the Supplemen-
tary Appendix). The analyses of treatment effects
on clinical progression-free survival according to
the volume of disease and planned early docetax-
el treatment showed consistently smaller effects
of enzalutamide in patients with high-volume
disease and in those with early docetaxel treat-
ment. However, P values for heterogeneity of the
treatment effect of enzalutamide were no longer
significant after adjustment for multiple com-
parisons (Figs. S2, S3, and S4 in the Supplemen-
tary Appendix).

Treatment after progression was initiated at the
discretion of the patients and their physicians.

Trial Oversight
The trial was led by the Australian and New
Zealand Urogenital and Prostate Cancer Trials
Group (ANZUP) and the National Health and
Medical Research Council (NHMRC) Clinical
Trials Centre, University of Sydney. Regional
sponsorship and coordination was performed by
Cancer Trials Ireland in Ireland and the United
Kingdom, the Canadian Cancer Trials Group in
Canada, and the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute
in the United States. The trial was designed by the
ANZUP investigators. Data were collected and
analyzed by the NHMRC Clinical Trials Centre.
The authors were solely responsible for the writ-
ing of the manuscript.
Astellas Pharma provided enzalutamide and
financial support for trial conduct; representa-
tives of the company reviewed drafts of the pro-
tocol and trial report but were not otherwise in-
volved in any aspects of the trial design, data
accrual, data analysis, or manuscript preparation.
Testosterone suppression, standard antiandrogen
drugs, docetaxel, and all subsequent treatments
were accessed according to local standard prac-
tice. The authors vouch for the accuracy and
completeness of the reported data and for the
fidelity of the trial to the protocol.
An independent data and safety monitoring
committee reviewed the progress and results of
the trial. The trial was conducted in accordance
with the principles of Good Clinical Practice
guidelines and the Declaration of Helsinki. The
protocol was independently reviewed and ap-
proved as required at each participating institu-
tion. All the patients provided written informed
consent.
End Points
The primary end point of overall survival was
measured as the interval from randomization to
death from any cause or to the date at which the
patient was last known to be alive. The second-
ary end point of PSA progression-free survival
was measured as the interval from randomiza-
tion to the earliest event of PSA progression ac-
cording to the criteria of the Prostate Cancer
Working Group 2 (a confirmed relative increase
in the PSA level from the nadir value by ≥25%
and by ≥2 ng per milliliter),18 clinical progres-
sion, death from any cause, or the last known
date of follow-up without PSA progression. The
secondary end point of clinical progression was
defined as the earliest sign of radiographic pro-
gression according to the criteria of the Prostate
Cancer Working Group 2 for bone lesions and
the Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tu-
mors, version 1.1,19 for soft-tissue lesions; the
development of symptoms attributable to cancer
progression; or the initiation of another antican-
cer treatment for prostate cancer. Imaging by
means of CT and bone scanning was recom-
mended to confirm clinical suspicion of pro-
gressive disease. Imaging reports (but not the
images themselves) were reviewed centrally. Ad-
verse events were graded according to the Na-
tional Cancer Institute Common Terminology
Criteria for Adverse Events, version 4.02. Ad-
verse-event data were collected during the treat-
ment period, with a final safety assessment
performed 30 to 42 days after the cessation of
the trial regimen.
Statistical Analysis
We determined that the enrollment of 1100 pa-
tients (with 470 deaths) would provide a power
of at least 80% to detect a 25% lower hazard of
death in the enzalutamide group than in the
standard-care group (hazard ratio, 0.75), with a
two-sided type I error rate of 0.05. In these cal-
culations, we assumed a 3-year survival rate of
65% in the standard-care group on the basis of
two previous studies of enzalutamide in men
with metastatic, castration-resistant prostate
cancer.15,16 Protocol versions 1 and 2 called for
an interim analysis of overall survival after the
occurrence of 67% of the prespecified 470
deaths with the use of the Lan-DeMets alpha-
spending function. Protocol version 3, which
was written after external evidence became
available for improved overall survival with early
abiraterone treatment,8,9 added interim analyses
of overall survival after the occurrence of 50%
and 80% of the prespecified 470 deaths. The
trial executive committee made these decisions
without any knowledge of outcomes in each
treatment group.

The baseline characteristics of all the patients
are summarized in Table 1 and detailed in the
Supplementary Appendix. High-volume disease
was present in 52% of the patients in the two
groups. Early docetaxel treatment was planned
in 45% of the patients (including in 61% of those
with high-volume disease and in 27% of those
with low-volume disease) but was not adminis-
tered to 22 patients, 11 in each of the randomly
assigned treatment groups. The full planned
course of six cycles of docetaxel was given to 159
of 243 patients (65%) in the enzalutamide group
and 181 of 238 (76%) in the standard-care group.
Overall Survival
The first interim analysis of the primary end
point occurred on February 28, 2019, after the
occurrence of 235 deaths. On March 7, 2019, the
independent data and safety monitoring com-
mittee recommended that the unblinded results
be provided to the trial executive committee so
that plans for definitive analyses could be imple-
mented. The observed P value of 0.0016 met the
rejection boundary of 0.0031 for the null hypoth-
esis that was specified for this interim analysis.
The results that are reported here include 10
additional deaths (for a total of 245) after a re-
view to ascertain the survival status of all the
patients as of February 28, 2019, after a median
follow-up of 34 months.
At the time of this analysis, there were 102
deaths in the enzalutamide group and 143 deaths
in the standard-care group (hazard ratio for
death, 0.67; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.52 to
0.86; P = 0.002) (Fig. 1A). The results were unaf-
fected by adjustments for geographical region,
volume of disease, use of early docetaxel treat-
ment, bone antiresorptive therapy, and coexisting
conditions. The median survival time was not yet
estimable in either trial group. The Kaplan-Meier
estimates of overall survival at 3 years were 80%
(based on 94 events) in the enzalutamide group
and 72% (based on 130 events) in the standard-
care group.
Progression-free Survival
The effects of enzalutamide on PSA progression-
free survival and clinical progression-free survival
were larger than its effect on overall survival. For
PSA progression-free survival, there were 174
events in the enzalutamide group and 333 events
in the standard-care group (rate of event-free
survival at 3 years, 67% and 37% respectively;
hazard ratio, 0.39; 95% CI, 0.33 to 0.47; P<0.001)
(Fig. 1B). For clinical progression-free survival,
there were 167 events in the enzalutamide group
and 320 events in the standard-care group (rate
of event-free survival at 3 years, 68% and 41%,
respectively; hazard ratio, 0.40; 95% CI, 0.33 to
0.49; P<0.001) (Fig. 1C). P values for analyses of
the between-group difference in PSA progres-
sion-free survival and clinical progression-free
survival remained highly significant after adjust-
ment for multiple comparisons.
Subgroup Analyses
The effects of enzalutamide on overall survival
were smaller among the patients in the stratified
subgroups with respect to bone antiresorptive
therapy, planned early docetaxel treatment, and
high-volume disease (Fig. 2, and Table S3 in the
Supplementary Appendix). After adjustment for
multiple comparisons, P values for heterogeneity
of the treatment effect of enzalutamide were
0.14 for volume of disease, 0.14 for early docetax-
el treatment, and 0.06 for the use of bone anti-
resorptive therapy.
We anticipated that the smaller number of
deaths would limit the reliability of subgroup
analyses of overall survival. Thus, we specified
in the analysis plan that subgroup analyses of
progression-free survival would also be per-
formed to take advantage of the larger number
of events for this secondary end point. The ef-
fects of enzalutamide on clinical progression-
free survival were noted in all predefined sub-
groups, including those with early docetaxel
treatment (Fig. 3, and Fig. S2 in the Supplemen-
tary Appendix). The analyses of treatment effects
on clinical progression-free survival according to
the volume of disease and planned early docetax-
el treatment showed consistently smaller effects
of enzalutamide in patients with high-volume
disease and in those with early docetaxel treat-
ment. However, P values for heterogeneity of the
treatment effect of enzalutamide were no longer
significant after adjustment for multiple com-
parisons (Figs. S2, S3, and S4 in the Supplemen-
tary Appendix).

discretion of the patients and their physicians.

- Randomization: Low
- Deviations from intended interventions: Low
- Missing outcome data: Low
- Outcome measurement: Low

Key considerations: the trial was open-label, but Overall Survival is an objective all-cause mortality outcome; efficacy used intention-to-treat analysis. Only 14 participants were lost to follow-up or withdrew consent and were censored. The early interim analysis could overestimate benefit, but the prespecified interim framework and external, outcome-independent amendment supported a Low selection-bias judgment.

Result: HR 0.67 (95% CI 0.52–0.86), 102 vs 143 deaths.
